Not quite. First think about a closed economic system where everybody starts with $100. If we call somebody rich who has 10x as much as everybody else then the max number of rich would be 10% and everybody else would have 0. If this isn't mathematically clear then simply imagine there are 100 people who start with $100 each. That's a total of $10,000. Somebody would be rich if they have $1000 so the max number of rich individual is 10. 10x as much wealth means 10% max rich people, 100x as much means 1% max rich people, etc. It's obvious that in closed systems any large chunk of people becoming rich is literally impossible.

Now ostensibly we don't have a closed economic system. Money is constantly being created out of thin air, primarily through bank loans. 97% of new money is created by banks, not the government. The way this works is fractional reserve lending. The US has a fractional reserve requirement of 10% for big banks meaning they only have to keep 10% of deposits on hand. That means when Joe deposits $100 at a bank that bank can then legally loan out $90 of that even if that $100 is all they have. If Joe comes back for his $100 it simply isn't there, which is the point of the central bank or US Federal Reserve also known as the Fed - they'd come save the day in case of a run on the bank. This multiplies money as Joe deposits $100 and $90 is loaned out. That $90 is deposited at another bank and then $81 is loaned out. That $81 is deposited and $73.10 is loaned out. And so on. That $100 deposit results in the creation of $1000 of new magical money.

But the catch here is that $1000 isn't actually money - it's debt. Our economic system is not closed, but the new money that comes in is created as debt. And the crazy part is that it's even more than $1000 of debt in our example. Banks not only lend out more money than they can cover, they also charge interest on those loans on top of it. That $1000 of debt might actually end up getting multiplied into several thousand dollars of debt. All based on a single modest initial "real" deposit of $100.

Our economic system is phenomenally complex, which is what keeps the dream alive. But ultimately suggesting that 54% (or anywhere near that) of people could become rich if they were smart enough and worked hard enough is simply false. Replace the entire world with Elon Musk's tomorrow and over the coming decades the economic distribution would not meaningfully change.

The good thing being that 53% of people do not have the capacity to be smart enough and work hard enough to obtain richness. Of course a model where there was would be absurd, though real life is more balanced.
